items.title: UK GDPR, Article 22C: Safeguards for automated decision-making
items.locator: Art. 22C(1) and 22C(2)(a); textual amendment note F1
items.why: The duty itself: safeguards must include measures that give the person information about significant, solely automated decisions taken about them. Says nothing on how detailed the information must be. Note F1: inserted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.80(1), fully in force 5 February 2026.
items.quote: provide the data subject with information about decisions described in paragraph 1 taken in relation to the data subject

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 15: Right of access by the data subject
items.locator: Art. 15(1)(h); note F4. Same wording at Art. 13(2)(f) and Art. 14(2)(g)
items.why: The separate transparency duty: the existence of automated decision-making subject to the Article 22C safeguards and, at least in those cases, meaningful information about the logic involved, its significance and envisaged consequences. Words substituted 5 February 2026.
items.quote: meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing for the data subject

items.title: Automated decision-making, including profiling (draft guidance): What are the ADM safeguards?
items.locator: Section 'What 'information about decisions' do we have to provide?'
items.why: Source of the quotation. Consultation draft published 31 March 2026; consultation closed 29 May 2026; final version not yet issued, so the wording may change. Lists what to include: contributing factors, whether profiling was involved, third-party data, how to ask for review.
items.quote: You should include an explanation of how and why you reached the decision about the specific person, and the impact on them.

items.title: Explaining decisions made with AI, Part 1: What goes into an explanation?
items.publisher: Information Commissioner's Office and The Alan Turing Institute
items.locator: 'At a glance' and section 'Process-based vs outcome-based explanations'
items.why: The six explanation types (rationale, responsibility, data, fairness, safety and performance, impact) and the process and outcome distinction. Under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 and still refers to Article 22. Year not shown on the page; to confirm.
items.quote: Outcome-based explanations of AI systems are about clarifying the results of a specific decision.

items.title: Explaining decisions made with AI, Part 3: Organisational roles and functions for explaining AI
items.publisher: Information Commissioner's Office and The Alan Turing Institute
items.locator: Section 'What if we use an AI system supplied by a third party?'
items.why: The controller keeps primary responsibility for making sure a bought-in system can produce an appropriate explanation. Under review, as above. Year not shown on the page; to confirm.
items.quote: you as the data controller have the primary responsibility for ensuring that the AI system you use is capable of producing an appropriate explanation

items.title: Project explAIn: interim report
items.publisher: Information Commissioner's Office and The Alan Turing Institute
items.locator: p. 10 (jury design: 18 jurors in Manchester, 18 in Coventry); p. 15 (findings by scenario)
items.why: Source of the figure. A small deliberative study, not a survey: it shows the value people place on an explanation depends on context. No percentages are given in this report.
items.quote: not a single juror concluded that an explanation should be provided in all contexts

items.title: AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), Article 86: Right to explanation of individual decision-making
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken
items.why: The EU's explicit right to an explanation from the deployer, for decisions based on high-risk systems listed in Annex III (except point 2) that a person considers adverse. Applies only where no other Union law already gives the right. The Commission's copy of the EUR-Lex consolidated text as at 27 July 2026; the application date for this article was not read and is not stated. Reaches UK firms only where they deploy such systems in the EU.

items.title: Regulation B (Equal Credit Opportunity Act), 12 CFR 1002.9: Notifications
items.locator: s.1002.9(b)(2), 'Statement of specific reasons', with official interpretation of paragraph 9(b)(2)
items.quote: must be specific and indicate the principal reason(s) for the adverse action
items.why: Comparator: the longest-standing binding rule against boilerplate. A US lender refusing credit must give the specific principal reasons; saying the applicant failed the lender's scoring system or internal policy is expressly 'insufficient'. The model for 'beyond boilerplate'. US federal rule for credit only; current text on the regulator's site, no date shown.

items.title: AI Update
items.quote: does not specifically address the transparency or explainability of AI systems
items.why: The financial regulator's position: no AI-specific explainability rule, but the Consumer Duty (good faith; meeting customers' information needs) and Principle 7 apply to firms using AI, alongside data protection law. A statement of approach, not rules. Written before the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025: it still describes Article 22. Date from the FCA's publication page.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in UK financial services - 2024
items.publisher: Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority
items.locator: Section 2.7, 'Explainability'; executive summary, 'Understanding of AI systems'
items.quote: A high proportion of firms currently using AI (81%) employ some kind of explainability method.
items.why: UK evidence on practice. Most firms use a technique such as feature importance, yet 46% reported only 'partial understanding' of the AI they use, largely because of third-party models. Having a method is not the same as being able to explain a decision to a customer. Survey of regulated financial firms only; self-reported.

items.title: Machine learning explainability in finance: an application to default risk analysis (Staff Working Paper No. 816)
items.publisher: Bank of England (Bracke, Datta, Jung and Sen)
items.locator: Abstract on the working paper's page
items.quote: This method investigates the inputs and outputs of the model, but not its inner workings.
items.why: UK working paper showing how the main factors behind a mortgage-default prediction can be estimated for a given case without opening the model, and that explanations differ markedly between groups of loans. Supports the 'main factors per decision' level. A staff working paper ('research in progress'), not peer reviewed; one model, one data set.

items.title: Four Principles of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (NISTIR 8312)
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.quote: We have termed these four principles as explanation, meaningful, explanation accuracy, and knowledge limits, respectively.
items.why: A free standard-setter's framework that gives testable properties for an explanation: it must exist, be understandable to the person receiving it, and reflect what the system really did. A basis for sampling explanation quality. Not a formal standard and not UK; ISO/IEC work on explainability is sold and could not be read.

items.title: Ethics, Transparency and Accountability Framework for Automated Decision-Making
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation, Cabinet Office and Office for Artificial Intelligence
items.locator: Point 5, 'Help users and citizens understand how it impacts them', under 'Context'
items.quote: you should be able to explain how the system reached that decision or suggested decision in plain English
items.why: The government's standard for its own departments: explanations in plain English, fitted to the audience and tested with end users. The only UK source found that asks for explanations to be iterated with the people who receive them. Guidance for central government, not binding on companies; date shown is the last update.

items.title: OECD AI Principles: Transparency and explainability (Principle 1.3)
items.quote: to provide plain and easy-to-understand information on the sources of data/input, factors, processes and/or logic that led to the prediction, content, recommendation or decision
items.why: International comparator. States what an explanation should contain (data sources, factors, logic) and that it should be plain, 'where feasible and useful'. The OECD's own page for the principle; the legal instrument itself (OECD/LEGAL/0449) could not be read because its site needs JavaScript, and the page shows no adoption or revision date. A non-binding recommendation to governments, not a rule for firms. Year is that of first adoption, from background knowledge.

items.title: Model Artificial Intelligence Governance Framework, Second Edition
items.publisher: Infocomm Media Development Authority and Personal Data Protection Commission, Singapore
items.quote: Organisations are encouraged to develop a policy on what explanations to provide to individuals and when to provide them.
items.why: Comparator from Singapore: asks for a written explanation policy and suggests the same standard of disclosure for AI-assisted decisions as for human ones. Matches the 'systematised explanation types' level. Voluntary and dated 2020.

items.title: Counterfactual Explanations without Opening the Black Box: Automated Decisions and the GDPR
items.publisher: Wachter, Mittelstadt and Russell, arXiv:1711.00399 (Harvard Journal of Law & Technology, 2018)
items.quote: to inform and help the individual understand why a particular decision was reached
items.why: Research that reframed explanation around what the person can do with it: understand, contest, and know what would need to change. The source of the 'what would have changed the outcome' form of explanation. Written on the EU GDPR before the UK's 2025 amendments; a legal and technical argument, not an empirical study.

items.title: Explainable Machine Learning in Deployment
items.quote: the majority of deployments are not for end users affected by the model but rather for machine learning engineers
items.why: Peer reviewed at a conference. A study of how organisations use explainability tools: most use them to debug models, not to explain decisions to the people affected. Evidence that a firm reporting 'we use explainability methods' may still have nothing to give a customer. Findings date from 2019.

items.title: Fooling LIME and SHAP: Adversarial Attacks on Post hoc Explanation Methods
items.publisher: Slack, Hilgard, Jia, Singh and Lakkaraju, arXiv:1911.02508
items.quote: post hoc explanations techniques that rely on input perturbations, such as LIME and SHAP, are not reliable
items.why: Shows a biased model can be built so that the two most widely used explanation tools report harmless reasons. Why explanation accuracy must be sampled and checked, not assumed. A constructed attack, not evidence that firms do this; the arXiv page read shows no publication venue.
